title: Agentic Orchestration & Finance Control Console: Building an Open Foundation for Agentic AI
summary: Learn how BlackLine is building an open, secure foundation for agentic AI in finance with Agentic Orchestration and the Finance Control Console. Read more.
body_markdown:
Key Takeaways


##


• AI-driven financial workflows require robust orchestration and governance to prevent compounding probabilistic errors in systems of record.


• Agentic Orchestration acts as the operating system for AI agents, while the Finance Control Console ensures human-in-the-loop oversight and compliance.


• BlackLine is open-sourcing its foundational specifications to establish common, vendor-agnostic industry standards for financial AI.


• A dual-surface execution layer combines the rapid data processing of AI with the situational intelligence and ethical oversight of human experts.


## Governing the Future of AI in Finance


Agentic Orchestration and Finance Control Console are central to the vision of BlackLine for Agentic Financial Operations. As foundational components of the BlackLine Agentic Financial Operations Platform, they work together to enable the coordinated execution, governance, and oversight of AI-driven financial workflows. Agentic Orchestration serves as the operating system for agentic execution, coordinating AI agents and workflows across financial systems, while Finance Control Console provides the governance, observability, and control needed to monitor agent activity, enforce policies, and maintain human oversight.


The BlackLine Agentic Financial Operations Platform is built to address urgent multi-dimensional challenges—technological, operational, regulatory, socio-ethical—emerging across industries, but one that is especially consequential for financial systems: leveraging the power of agentic AI while ensuring the safety, security, reliability, and regulatory compliance that are the non-negotiable fundamentals of any financial solution.


That is, how to safely and effectively harness the transformational gains in efficiency and breadth of solutions enabled by the speed and power of agentic AI decisions and actions at scale, while accounting for the inherently probabilistic and statistical nature of the large language models (LLMs) that power AI agents.


To understand this challenge, it is worth looking more closely at how AI agents operate. An AI agent that drives financial decision-making cannot inherently provide deterministic execution guarantees because the actions it generates are outputs of a stochastic approximation function rather than a deterministic rule engine. Large language models produce tool calls by sampling from learned conditional probability distributions over token sequences. Even under greedy (temperature-zero) decoding, the model’s mapping from context to a structurally and semantically correct function name, parameter schema, and parameter value remains a high-dimensional neural approximation that carries a finite, formally non-zero probability of error at every inference step. These errors can manifest as incorrect tool selection, hallucinated parameter values, misapplied business logic, or incorrect numerical operands.


Additionally, in a long-running and/or multi-step agentic automation the eventual outcome may suffer considerably because of the collective impact of the individual errors. In a multi-step agentic workflow built using an LLM with a generalized average error probability of ε per inference, these per-step errors can compound. Assuming independent steps with per-step accuracy of (1 − ε), an agent executing N sequential decisions achieves an end-to-end correctness probability of (1 − ε)N . in the context of financial workflows used by the Office of the CFO, even a small probability of error in a single LLM call can carry significant risk if allowed to propagate unchecked through a chain of financial decision-making. Numerical inaccuracies, incorrect assumptions, or misapplied logic can affect subsequent steps in an agentic workflow.


To demonstrate, consider an agent that prepares and posts the month-end accrual for an unbilled consulting engagement in six steps: retrieve the statement of work, read the hours delivered, calculate the amount, choose the expense and accrual accounts, set the entity and period, and post the entry. If the agent is right 99% of the time at each step, the chance that all six are right is about 94%, so across a[close](https://www.blackline.com/products/financial-close/) of 200 such entries, roughly a dozen will carry an error somewhere. A mistake at each step produces a balanced, properly formatted, self-consistent[journal](https://www.blackline.com/products/financial-close/journals/) that passes traditional system validation, so nothing flags it. At the last step, the agent posts the entry in the system of record, which now will persist those incorrect entries, eventually leading to material weakness in the reported results and subsequent audit failures.


Agentic Orchestration and Finance Control Console complement each other by providing the safeguards, observability, and human oversight needed to manage these types of risks across financial workflows. The orchestration platform ensures that all agentic computations/conclusions are evaluated against pre-defined thresholds for accuracy and acceptability, and human-in-the-loop judgment is mandated when those thresholds are not met. Agents themselves are not allowed to directly mutate financial records, automated mutations in a workflow must always go through these threshold-based policy enforcements. Additionally, Control Console provides a deep, context-aware insight into every step of such an orchestrated automation workflow including detailed explanations for agentic recommendations and decision matrix. In the example above, each of those dozen or so mistakes would be caught as thresholds not being met, necessitating human interventions and corrections before the eventual posting is performed for all the entries.


The world of finance and accounting within the office of the CFO is already being transformed by LLMs and AI agents, with an increasing focus on automating repetitive tasks. The ability to quickly build agents using skills and connectors offered by agentic technology vendors enables finance organizations to rapidly develop and deploy these ad hoc agents, even outside the context of any centralized workflow orchestration. When these agents operate outside established workflow automation systems, they can become ungoverned AI actors, making decisions and even modifying financial systems of record on behalf of human employees. This presents challenges of the same magnitude associated with multi-step agentic workflows, particularly around visibility, accountability, and control.


Finance Control Console offers a foundational, vendor-agnostic approach to bringing visibility, observability, monitoring, and control to these agents, including those developed without centralized oversight or a full appreciation of the risks they may introduce. By providing a consistent framework for governance across both orchestrated workflows and independently developed agents, Finance Control Console helps organizations maintain the oversight necessary as their agentic ecosystems expand.


## Specifications and Schema


Agentic Orchestration and Finance Control Console are built on a central premise, informed by more than 20 years of domain expertise from BlackLine in the Office of the CFO, its experience developing and implementing Verity AI capabilities, and its research into the mechanics of agentic AI: safety, governance, predictability, and auditability must be inherent properties of any platform that enables financial workflows incorporating AI agents. These cannot be an afterthought.


Secondly, given the diverse spectrum of traditional ERP systems and operational platforms used by the office of the CFO, alongside the rapidly evolving landscape of agentic technologies and LLM modalities, including multiple frontier model vendors, privately hosted models, and tuned open-weight models, Agentic Orchestration and Finance Control Console **,** we envision these systems built around a normalized set of foundational specifications and API schemas that are vendor- and technology-agnostic. These foundational specifications and schemas reflect the prescriptive and opinionated approach of BlackLine – informed by insights collected from regulators, audit firms and from serving large enterprises—to how agents and agentic workflows should be configured, run, managed, governed, and audited within the office of the CFO.


While BlackLine is building its Agentic Financial Operations Platform with foundational semantic primitives that conform to these specifications, we anticipate other vendors developing their own implementations of agentic orchestration and governance capabilities, tailored to their respective use cases. Moreover, the core concepts and underlying architectural principles governing these specifications can be extended to ecosystems of agents operating in other domains.


The generality of these specifications and schemas reflects a fundamental shift in the nature of software as agentic AI evolves. Software is moving beyond interfaces designed primarily for human interaction, or even human-AI interaction, toward an execution layer built for both autonomous agents and human oversight. The scope of human oversight in such a dual-surface execution layer extends beyond the binary approval or rejection of an agent’s recommendation, enabling a more nuanced model of human-agent collaboration. Human judgment brings situation-specific intelligence developed through years of lived experience, socio-ethical awareness of when optimization should or should not determine a decision, rational skepticism, and an understanding of the human consequences of certain types of mistakes. These uniquely human capabilities can be applied alongside the strengths of AI agents, which excel at rapidly exploring a broad range of possibilities informed by extensive prior knowledge.


The directed acyclic graph (DAG) that describes the Agentic Orchestration workflow schema enables this dual-execution surface through a defined taxonomy of DAG nodes and an explicit sequence connecting agentic nodes, policy evaluation, and human-in-the-loop intervention. The threshold for human intervention can be configured using the Policy node, allowing organizations to determine when agentic execution can proceed autonomously and when human judgment or approval is required. The precise manner in which these nodes are connected, along with the permitted action paths, constitutes a grammatical invariant of the schema and embodies one of the core tenets of the BlackLine vision for agentic governance.


Similarly, the contracts and entities within these schemas and specifications reflect our vision for agentic orchestration, automation, governance, and audit. Our internal implementation will continue to conform to these specifications, and customers will be able to interact with Agentic Orchestration and Finance Control Console through the specifications and API schemas, just as they can through the BlackLine Platform’s user interfaces.


At the same time, the schemas remain extensible and adaptable. For example, we define a rich and generalized syntax for telemetry events across the agentic ecosystem while ensuring compatibility with CloudEvents, a widely adopted specification across multiple domains. This approach enables the underlying specifications to accommodate evolving technologies and use cases without compromising the consistency of the orchestration and governance framework.


## Open Specifications


Why open source these specifications at all? The answer lies in how agentic AI is being adopted within the office of the CFO. Finance organizations today procure AI capabilities from multiple vendors, deploy agents embedded within different applications, and increasingly build their own agents using readily available models and connectors. As a result, organizations will operate a heterogeneous population of agents, each orchestrated, permissioned, and logged in its own way.


Without a common set of semantics for how these agents are orchestrated and governed, that heterogeneity can lead to fragmentation: agents acting independently under inconsistent governance practices, executing decisions, and even modifying financial systems of record without consistent visibility or oversight. For finance leaders, this raises questions of financial integrity and auditability. For IT leaders, it creates challenges in governing agent behavior and system access across an increasingly diverse technology landscape. And because the potential for compounding errors in agentic workflows does not respect vendor or technology boundaries, we believe an open specification for orchestration and governance offers a collaborative and efficient pathway toward establishing common industry standards.


Such specifications would provide a clear separation between a comprehensive, semantically consistent representational layer and the heterogeneous, rapidly evolving technologies used to build and run agents and workflows. This is precisely why we believe the foundational principles for orchestrating and governing AI agents within the office of the CFO should not be proprietary to any single vendor, and why open sourcing the Agentic Orchestration and Finance Control Console specifications is a natural extension of our design philosophy.


An open, normalized set of specifications and API schemas, spanning vendor-agnostic orchestration, policy-driven execution, human-agent collaboration, observability, auditability, and extensibility, allows the broader community to converge on common semantics for how agentic workflows are configured, run, governed, and audited, while every vendor remains free to innovate and differentiate through its own implementation. The specifications prescribe the grammar, not the implementation or the technology stack.


For IT organizations, this creates opportunities for interoperability and architectural flexibility across frontier, privately hosted, and open-weight models alike. For the office of the CFO, it means AI capabilities can operate within a consistent framework of accountability and oversight, regardless of where those capabilities originate. We believe a challenge of this scale and consequence is best addressed through industry collaboration rather than isolated efforts. The future of agentic AI should not be defined by any single technology provider, but built on a foundation of trust that the broader industry can help advance.


We invite others building or planning to build agentic orchestration and governance solutions to consider adopting these specifications and schemas as the semantic fabric of their solutions, and to participate in public discussions around extending, modifying, and enhancing them. By working together to establish common principles for orchestration, governance, and auditability, we can help create an agentic ecosystem that supports continued innovation while maintaining the accountability and oversight that financial operations demand.


The specifications are open sourced in a BlackLine-maintained GitHub repository, under the Apache 2.0 license, and the open-source community can contribute following the conventional mechanism of fork-change-validate-pull request. There are concrete guidelines around backwards compatibility, vendor neutrality, documentation, commit message convention. The detailed contribution guidelines are included in the repository README file.
